description:
We’re tackling “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” using NASA data to find what’s changing on Earth, where, by how much, and whether it’s statistically significant. Before trusting any trend, we’ll check the data for gaps and suspicious jumps, as a security tester would.

Looking for: Python/data analysis, data visualization, Earth science or statistics, and design or presentation skills.

All levels welcome. Send a request to join!
summary:
Telemetry Watchdog is a trend detective that checks its own evidence. It analyzes six NASA datasets (nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) from OMI, aerosol optical depth (AOD) from MODIS, and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) from MERRA-2) for Los Angeles and New York City from 2005 to 2025. For each one, it answers the four questions the challenge asks: what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant.
Before trusting any trend, the tool screens the data for missing dates, duplicate records, physically impossible values, and sudden spikes, then gives each dataset a trust score. It also records a SHA-256 fingerprint of every file, so any later change to the data can be detected. Its key feature is that it reports every trend twice: once with all data and once without the flagged records. If the conclusion changes, the data-quality problem matters. If it does not, the trend is robust.
In our results, all six trends were significant and robust. NO₂ fell about 41% per decade in both cities, while PM2.5 in Los Angeles was the only variable that increased.
This matters because climate and air-quality decisions rely on trends, and a trend built on faulty measurements can point in the wrong direction. Telemetry Watchdog makes that risk visible. It delivers a self-contained HTML report with interactive charts that opens in any browser.
details:
What it does
Telemetry Watchdog finds long-term trends in NASA Earth observation data and then tests whether each trend can be trusted. Most trend tools give you a line and a number. Ours checks the data first, gives each dataset a trust score, and reports every trend twice: once with all data and once without the flagged records. If the conclusion changes, the data problem matters. If it doesn’t, the trend is robust. For each dataset it answers the challenge’s four questions: what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant.

How it works
We downloaded six datasets from NASA Giovanni for Los Angeles and New York City, January 2005 to September 2026: tropospheric NO₂ (OMI), aerosol optical depth (MODIS Aqua), and surface PM2.5 (MERRA-2). The tool works in four steps:

  1. Reading: It reads each CSV, takes the fill value (“no data”) from the file header, and counts unreadable lines.
  2. Checking: It looks for missing dates, duplicate and out-of-order dates, physically impossible values (such as negative concentrations), extreme values (more than 8 robust standard deviations from the usual level for that calendar month), and isolated one-day spikes. It records a SHA-256 fingerprint of every file, so any later change to the data is detected.
  3. Scoring: The trust score is the percentage of measured values with no flag. Coverage is the percentage of days or months that have a measurement.
  4. Trend testing: It uses the seasonal Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope on monthly means for 2005–2025, leaving out 2026 because it’s incomplete. Each month is compared only with the same month in other years, so summer-versus-winter swings are not mistaken for a trend.

Results
The tool read 32,194 rows and found 20,596 valid measurements. It flagged 390 of them, and trust scores ranged from 91% to 100%. All six trends are statistically significant (p < 0.05), and all six stay the same when the flagged records are removed. NO₂ fell about 41% per decade in both cities. AOD fell 8.6% per decade in Los Angeles and 15% in New York. PM2.5 fell 2.8% per decade in New York but rose 3.9% per decade in Los Angeles, the only increase we found. The tool also surfaced things a normal analysis would miss:

  • All 9 flagged PM2.5 months in Los Angeles are unusually high and line up with wildfire periods, including the 2009 Station Fire, September 2020, and January 2025. The upward trend holds even without them.
  • On July 7, 2010, Los Angeles AOD reached 4.76, 38 robust standard deviations above normal for July. The tool marks it for review instead of silently keeping or deleting it.
  • New York AOD had the lowest trust score (91%), mostly because of values below zero.

Benefits and intended impact
Students, citizen scientists, and researchers can see not only what the trend is but how much to trust it. The report explains every result in plain sentences, lists every flagged record with its date, CSV line, and reason, and links back to the exact Giovanni request so anyone can reproduce the data. We want “check the evidence” to become a normal step in trend analysis, before results get shared or acted on.

Tools and technology
NASA Giovanni; OMI OMNO2d v004, MODIS-Aqua MYD08_D3 v6.1, MERRA-2 M2TMNXAER v5.12.4; Python in Visual Studio; Plotly for the interactive charts; a self-contained HTML report that works offline in any browser; GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting.

Creativity
Our team is called Ethical Hackers in Space, and we treated the data the way a security tester treats input: never trusted until it’s checked. Like file-integrity monitoring in cybersecurity, the tool fingerprints every file it uses. Instead of only finding trends, it tries to break its own findings and reports honestly whether they hold up.

Factors our team considered
A flagged value is unusual, not necessarily wrong. Wildfire smoke is real, so we flag it but don’t delete it. Satellite column measurements are not the same as air quality at ground level, and MERRA-2 uses satellite AOD as an input, so the two sources are not fully independent. A fingerprint shows that a file hasn’t changed, but it doesn’t prove where the file came from. Nearby months are correlated, which can make p-values slightly too small. A significant trend shows a consistent change, not its cause. Two cities are a case study, not a global result. We also wanted the report to be readable by non-experts, not just statisticians.

Future Enhancements

Right now Telemetry Watchdog checks CSV files. The next step is to have it validate live data pulled straight from NASA’s open APIs. One example is the NASA POWER API, which returns daily weather values for any point on Earth in JSON format. A request like https://power.larc.nasa.gov/api/temporal/daily/point?parameters=RH2M,T2M&community=RE&latitude=34.05&longitude=-118.24&start=20261001&end=20261031&format=JSON gets October 2026 relative humidity and temperature for Los Angeles. The Watchdog could run its missing-value, duplicate and out-of-range checks on that data as soon as it arrives. Adding context variables would also let the tool explain an anomaly instead of only flagging it. Relative humidity (RH) matters because aerosol particles absorb water and swell in humid air. That can raise MODIS aerosol optical depth (AOD) even when no extra pollution is present, so the Watchdog could tag a spike that happens during high RH as “possibly humidity-driven” rather than a real pollution event. Planetary boundary layer height (PBLH) is available from NASA’s MERRA-2 reanalysis through GES DISC using an Earthdata Login. It shows how much air pollution can mix into. When the boundary layer is shallow, as during winter inversions over the Los Angeles basin, NO₂ and aerosols get trapped near the ground. In those cases, satellite readings of the whole air column often don’t match what ground monitors measure. Adding PBLH would help the tool handle problems researchers still haven’t fully solved, such as turning satellite AOD into reliable estimates of ground-level PM2.5 and explaining why NO₂ trends from satellites and ground stations sometimes disagree. Finally, to keep the project’s cybersecurity focus, future versions could store a checksum and source details for every file they download. That way the Watchdog could catch data that was corrupted or changed between NASA’s servers and the user’s analysis, which fits our tagline: “Trust your data before you trust your results.”

Known Caveats: What the Tool Does Not Claim

Telemetry Watchdog tells you how much to trust a trend. It does not tell you everything about it. Here is what our results do not mean:

A flag does not mean a value is wrong. A flag means the value is unusual. Wildfire smoke, for example, is real, so we flag those months but never delete them. Every result is shown both with and without flagged records so readers can decide for themselves.

A trend does not explain its cause. A significant trend shows that a change is consistent over time. It does not show why the change happened, such as emission rules, fuel changes, wildfires or weather.

Satellite data is not the same as the air people breathe. OMI NO₂ and MODIS AOD measure the whole column of air above a city, not air quality at ground level.

Our datasets are not fully independent. MERRA-2 PM2.5 uses satellite AOD as an input, so when the AOD and PM2.5 results agree, that is not two separate confirmations.

The p-values may be slightly too optimistic. Nearby months are related to each other, which can make p-values a little smaller than they should be. Trends with very small p-values are less affected.

A fingerprint proves a file has not changed, not where it came from. The SHA-256 fingerprint detects any change to a file after we downloaded it. It cannot prove the file came from NASA. That is why we link to the exact Giovanni request, so anyone can download the same data again.

Two cities are a case study, not a global result. Los Angeles and New York show how the method works. They do not show what is happening in other cities or worldwide.

Negative AOD may not be an error. MODIS AOD retrievals can legitimately be slightly below zero (as far as I know, the product allows values down to about −0.05). If New York’s 91% score comes mostly from those values, a NASA judge may see it as a bug in your tool. Check the MYD08_D3 documentation. Then treat small negative values as “valid but low noise” and flag only values below the product’s allowed range.

Check the NO₂ number. “41% per decade” over 20 years implies a total drop of roughly 80%, which is large for OMI. Recheck how you turn Sen’s slope into a percentage, and say what the baseline is (for example, the 2005 mean or the period mean).

OMI has a known detector problem from 2007 onward. Adding it to “Factors considered” shows you know the instrument.

In short: Telemetry Watchdog checks whether a trend survives problems in the data. It does not replace expert judgment, ground-level monitoring or research into causes.
